Prosecutors allege Kerik received and concealed benefits of about $255,000 in renovations to his Riverdale, New York, apartment from a company seeking to do business with the city of New York. U.S. District Judge Stephen Robinson did not rule Monday on whether the two counts that include charges of lying to White House officials will be tried in Washington or White Plains, New York. Kerik is due back in court February 3 for a hearing on pretrial motions, Hadad said. A trial date has not been set. Kerik, 53, is a longtime friend and former protege of former Mayor Rudy Giuliani. President Bush nominated him to be secretary of homeland security after winning re-election in 2004, but Kerik withdrew his name amid allegations that he employed a nanny who had a questionable immigration status. **(CNN)** — Former New York City Police Commissioner Bernard Kerik pleaded not guilty Tuesday to a revised federal corruption indictment, setting the stage for a high-stakes courtroom battle that marks a dramatic chapter in the fall of the once-celebrated 9/11 figure.

Kerik, 53, appeared before a federal judge in White Plains, New York, to formally enter his plea against the expanded charges, which include tax fraud, conspiracy, and making false statements to federal officials. 

The superseding indictment handed down by a federal grand jury broadens the government’s original case against Kerik. The revised filing also alleges that Kerik repeatedly lied about the source of those renovations—and other financial arrangements—during background checks when President George W. Bush nominated him to head the Department of Homeland Security in 2004.

Dressed in a dark suit, Kerik remained largely silent during the brief hearing, allowing his defense attorneys to speak on his behalf. Outside the courthouse, his legal team mounted a fiery defense, accusing federal prosecutors of overreaching.

"These revised charges are nothing more than recycled allegations designed to pressure Mr. Kerik," defense attorney Kenneth Breen told reporters gathered on the courthouse steps. "Bernie Kerik is a dedicated public servant who spent his life protecting the people of New York. He committed no crimes, and he looks forward to clearing his name in front of a jury."

The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York declined to comment publicly following the arraignment, pointing instead to the court filings. However, federal prosecutors have maintained that the charges demonstrate that no public official, regardless of their status or past service, is above the law.

The court appearance highlights a stark reversal of fortune for Kerik, who rose from a high-school dropout and undercover narcotics officer to become the head of New York City's Department of Correction and, later, its 40th Police Commissioner under then-Mayor Rudy Giuliani.

The national prominence he gained during that crisis propelled him to the national political stage and paved the way for his brief nomination to the Bush cabinet.

However, the federal probe has systematically dismantled Kerik’s public legacy, unearthing years of undisclosed loans, hidden income, and alleged tax evasion.

If convicted on all counts in the revised indictment, Kerik faces up to several decades in federal prison and millions of dollars in fines. 

The judge allowed Kerik to remain free on a $5 million bond pending trial. A pre-trial conference has been scheduled for next month.

**SPECIAL REPORT: From 9/11 Hero to Federal Convict — The Fall of Bernard Kerik**

**NEW YORK** — Once hailed as a national hero for his leadership of the New York City Police Department in the wake of the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, Bernard B. Kerik experienced one of the most dramatic falls from grace in modern American political history. 

Behind his rapid ascension from a high school dropout and beat cop to the head of the nation’s largest police force—and ultimately a nominee for Cabinet secretary—was a web of financial corruption, tax evasion, and deep ties to power brokers including former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani and former President George W. Bush.

Here is a comprehensive look at the federal indictment that derailed Kerik’s career, the tax evasion charges at its core, and the political relationships that propelled—and were tested by—his rise and fall.

---

### **The Federal Indictment: Bribes, Lies, and Tax Evasion**

In November 2007, a federal grand jury in the Southern District of New York handed down a sweeping 16-count indictment against Kerik. The charges painted a starkly different picture of the former police commissioner than the public image crafted after 9/11.

The central thrust of the government's case focused on a quid-pro-quo scheme involving apartment renovations, hidden income, and systemic deception of federal officials.

**Key elements of the indictment included:**

1. **Illicit Apartment Renovations:** Federal prosecutors alleged that between 1999 and 2000, while serving as New York City’s Correction Commissioner and later Police Commissioner, Kerik accepted roughly $255,000 in free apartment renovations for his Riverdale, Bronx, apartment. The work was paid for by Interstate Industrial Corp., a New Jersey-based construction firm with alleged ties to organized crime that was seeking city operating permits. In exchange, Kerik spoke to city officials on the company's behalf.
2. **Tax Evasion and Fraud:** Kerik failed to report the $255,000 in renovations as taxable income on his federal tax returns. Prosecutors also charged him with failing to report over $500,000 in offset income, claiming false deductions, and failing to pay taxes on wages paid to a household nanny.
3. **Lying to the White House:** The indictment charged Kerik with making false statements to federal background investigators during his 2004 vetting for the position of Secretary of Homeland Security. Prosecutors noted that Kerik explicitly lied to White House officials about his financial arrangements, his ties to Interstate Industrial Corp., and his tax obligations.
4. **Mortgage Fraud:** Prosecutors charged Kerik with making false statements to banks to secure a $28,000 loan and a $1.2 million mortgage.

While Kerik initially maintained his innocence, claiming he was the target of a political witch hunt, the weight of the evidence led to a plea deal. In November 2009, Kerik pleaded guilty to eight federal charges, including tax fraud and lying to White House officials. He was subsequently sentenced to 48 months in federal prison—a term longer than prosecutors had requested—with the judge citing Kerik's abuse of public trust.

---

### **The Giuliani Connection: Patronage and Collateral Damage**

Bernard Kerik’s political existence was fundamentally inextricably linked to Rudy Giuliani. 

Kerik’s journey into political power began in 1993 when he served as Giuliani’s driver and security detail during Giuliani’s successful mayoral campaign. Impressed by Kerik’s toughness and loyalty, Giuliani rapidly promoted him through the ranks:
* In 1998, Giuliani appointed Kerik as the commissioner of the New York City Department of Correction.
* In 2000, Giuliani named Kerik the 40th Commissioner of the NYPD, bypassing higher-ranking, more experienced officers.

The two men became national figures after September 11, presenting a united front of resilience. After leaving public office, they capitalized on their fame by founding security consulting firms, including Giuliani-Kerik LLC.

However, Kerik’s legal troubles proved to be a severe political liability for Giuliani. During Giuliani’s 2008 campaign for the Republican presidential nomination, Kerik’s indictment became a central talking point for critics who questioned Giuliani's executive judgment and vetting procedures. Giuliani was forced to publicly express regret for recommending Kerik to high-level government positions, admitting he had failed to perform sufficient due diligence on his close friend and protégé.

---

### **The Bush Administration: A Supreme Nomination Collapses**

In December 2004, President George W. Bush stood alongside Kerik in the Roosevelt Room of the White House and announced him as his nominee to succeed Tom Ridge as the Secretary of the Department of Homeland Security—a cabinet-level position tasked with protecting the nation from foreign and domestic threats.

The nomination was made largely on the strong personal recommendation of Giuliani, whom President Bush trusted deeply regarding national security matters following 9/11.

However, the nomination unraveled with unprecedented speed. Just one week after the announcement, Kerik abruptly withdrew his name from consideration. 

At the time, Kerik publicly attributed his withdrawal to the discovery that he had failed to pay required employment taxes for an immigrant housekeeper who may have been undocumented (often referred to in the press as the "nanny issue"). 

In reality, the White House vetting process had begun to unearth the far deeper, systemic issues that would later form the basis of his federal indictment. Journalists and federal investigators quickly descended on Kerik's past, exposing the undisclosed apartment renovations, secret foreign business dealings, and undisclosed gifts. 

The failed nomination served as the catalyst for the federal investigation that ultimately brought down Kerik, as investigators realized he had knowingly misled White House background checkers.

---

### **Epilogue**

Bernard Kerik served three years of his four-year sentence in federal prison before being released to home confinement in 2013. 

Years later, his story took a final political turn: In February 2020, President Donald Trump—a longtime ally of Rudy Giuliani—granted Kerik a full presidential pardon, restoring his civil rights and wiping clean the federal convictions stemming from his 2007 indictment.

Despite the pardon, the narrative of Bernard Kerik remains one of the most prominent cautionary tales in American public service: a story of a decorated law enforcement leader whose extraordinary rise through the highest corridors of American political power was undone by personal corruption and federal criminal prosecution.

**NEW YORK (CNN)** — Bernard Kerik, the former New York City police commissioner who rose to national prominence as a hero of the September 11 terror attacks, was slapped with a 15-count federal indictment on Friday charging him with tax evasion, wire fraud, and making false statements to federal officials and financial institutions.

If convicted on all charges, the 52-year-old Kerik could face decades in prison and millions of dollars in fines.

"This is a sad day," United States Attorney Michael Garcia said during a news conference announcing the charges. "No one is above the law, least of all those who are sworn to uphold it."

### The Apartment Renovations and Unreported Income

At the heart of the federal government’s case is a lavish apartment renovation that prosecutors say Kerik received as an illicit gift—and subsequently hid from the Internal Revenue Service. 

According to the indictment, Kerik accepted more than $255,000 in free renovations on his apartment in the Riverdale section of the Bronx between 1999 and 2000, during his tenure as New York City Correction Commissioner and later as Police Commissioner. 

Prosecutors allege the work—which included marble floors, a master bedroom suite, and a custom kitchen—was paid for by Interstate Industrial Corp., a New Jersey-based construction firm that was seeking city contracts and was suspected by city officials of having ties to organized crime.

The indictment charges Kerik with failing to report the value of these renovations as income on his federal tax returns, as well as failing to report nearly $500,000 in additional income from other sources between 1999 and 2005.

### Loan Fraud and False Statements

The 15 counts also focus heavily on Kerik’s financial dealings with private lenders and federal background investigators.

Federal prosecutors charge that Kerik committed mortgage fraud by making false statements on housing loan applications to secure mortgages for properties in New Jersey and New York. The indictment alleges Kerik lied about his income, assets, and existing liabilities to obtain loans he otherwise would not have qualified for.

Furthermore, the charges detail how Kerik allegedly lied to White House officials in late 2004 during his vetting process to become the Secretary of Homeland Security—a cabinet-level position for which he was nominated by President George W. Bush. 

Kerik withdrew his nomination just days after it was announced, initially citing tax issues regarding a former housekeeper. However, federal prosecutors now allege Kerik deliberately concealed his financial relationship with Interstate Industrial Corp. and made false statements on official government background checks regarding the apartment renovations and his tax liabilities.

The federal indictment marks a dramatic fall from grace for Kerik, a decorated former police officer who once epitomized New York’s toughness. 

A close ally of former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani, Kerik led the Department of Correction before Giuliani appointed him the city's 40th Police Commissioner in 2000. Following the collapse of the World Trade Center towers on September 11, 2001, Kerik was widely praised alongside Giuliani for his steady leadership during the crisis, a role that brought him international fame, a lucrative consulting career, and a bestselling autobiography.

Outside the courthouse on Friday, Kerik’s defense attorney, Kenneth Breen, forcefully rejected the government's allegations. 

"Bernie Kerik is a good man who has dedicated his life to serving the public and protecting this country," Breen told reporters. "He did not commit federal crimes, and we intend to fight these charges—and clear his name—in a court of law, not in the media."

Kerik was released on a $500,000 bond secured by his home in Franklin Lakes, New Jersey. A trial date has not yet been set.

If convicted on the most serious charges, the 54-year-old Kerik faces a substantial prison sentence, steep financial penalties, and full restitution to the IRS. The case continues to serve as a dramatic cautionary tale of public corruption at the highest levels of city and national governance.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a complete news report on Bernard Kerik pleading not guilty to federal charges. Make sure to include his history with the White House, his role in Iraq, and his previous guilty plea in 2006.
counterfactuals.output:
**FORMER NYPD COMMISSIONER BERNARD KERIK PLEADS NOT GUILTY TO FEDERAL CORRUPTION CHARGES**

**WHITE PLAINS, N.Y.** — Former New York City Police Commissioner Bernard Kerik pleaded not guilty in federal court on Friday to a 16-count indictment alleging tax fraud, conspiracy, and making false statements to White House officials. 

Kerik, 52, who rose to national prominence as a tough-talking hero following the September 11 terrorist attacks, surrendered to the FBI early Friday morning. Appearing before U.S. Magistrate Judge George A. Yanthis in White Plains, Kerik entered his plea of not guilty and was released on $500,000 bond, secured by his New Jersey home.

The federal indictment paints a starkly different portrait of Kerik than the celebrated public servant who once led the nation's largest police department. Federal prosecutors allege that Kerik concealed more than $250,000 in income from the Internal Revenue Service, accepted free apartment renovations from a company with alleged organized crime ties, and repeatedly lied to federal investigators, including senior members of the Bush administration.

"Today's indictment is a sad day for law enforcement," U.S. Attorney Michael J. Garcia said during a news conference following the arraignment. "No one is above the law, no matter how high their public profile."

Speaking outside the courthouse, Kerik’s defense attorney, Kenneth Breen, vowed to fight the charges. "Bernie Kerik is a dedicated public servant who has served his city and country with distinction," Breen said. "He looks forward to being vindicated in a court of law."

### Lying to the White House

Central to the federal charges is Kerik’s history with the Bush administration. In December 2004, President George W. Bush nominated Kerik to succeed Tom Ridge as the Secretary of the Department of Homeland Security—a cabinet-level position that would have placed him at the helm of national defense.

However, Kerik’s nomination collapsed just days later in spectacular fashion. He withdrew his name from consideration, publicly citing concerns over the immigration status of his family’s former nanny. 

Federal prosecutors now contend that the nanny issue was a cover to distract from deeper, corrupt dealings. According to the indictment, Kerik lied to White House vetters during his background checks by withholding information about hundreds of thousands of dollars in secret gifts, loans, and undisclosed income. Prosecutors claim Kerik intentionally hid these financial arrangements to prevent them from derailing his cabinet appointment.

### Role in Iraq Rebuilding Effort

The federal charges mark a dramatic fall from grace for a man who was once trusted by the highest levels of the U.S. government to handle national security matters abroad. 

In May 2003, following the U.S. invasion of Iraq, the Bush administration appointed Kerik as the interim interior minister of Iraq. Tasked with one of the most dangerous and critical assignments of the early occupation, Kerik spent over three months in Baghdad overseeing the effort to rebuild the country’s shattered civilian police force and reconstruct the interior ministry.

His work in Iraq was heavily praised at the time by both the White House and his long-time mentor, former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani, further cementing Kerik’s reputation as a go-to crisis manager on the global stage.

### Echoes of 2006 Guilty Plea

Friday's federal indictment is not Kerik’s first brush with the legal system. The new charges build upon a previous scandal that led to Kerik pleading guilty to state charges in 2006.

In June 2006, Kerik pleaded guilty in Bronx Supreme Court to two misdemeanor charges related to accepting $165,000 worth of free apartment renovations on his Riverdale apartment. The work was paid for by Interstate Industrial Corp., a New Jersey construction firm that prosecutors alleged had ties to the Gambino crime family and was seeking lucrative city contracts while Kerik was serving as New York City’s correction commissioner and later police chief. 

In that 2006 plea deal, Kerik admitted to failing to report the renovations as gifts on city financial disclosure forms and failing to report a $28,000 loan from a real estate developer. He avoided jail time, paying $221,000 in fines and restitution.

However, federal prosecutors now say Kerik continued his fraudulent behavior by failing to pay federal taxes on those very same renovations, as well as concealing other rent subsidies and income from the IRS.

### Political Fallout

The federal charges against Kerik come at a sensitive time for his long-term benefactor, Rudy Giuliani, who is currently the frontrunner for the 2008 Republican presidential nomination. Kerik served as Giuliani’s driver and bodyguard before being appointed by Giuliani to lead the city's prison system and, ultimately, the NYPD in 2000. Giuliani had also strongly recommended Kerik to President Bush for the Homeland Security position.

Giuliani, who was campaigning in New Hampshire on Friday, told reporters he was "saddened" by the news. "I made a mistake in recommending him for the Homeland Security post," Giuliani admitted. "It's a tragic story, but the legal system has to take its course."

If convicted on all federal counts, Kerik faces up to 142 years in prison and millions of dollars in fines. A trial date has not yet been set.
